topics.title: Internet Standards
topics.definition: Internet standards are agreed specifications that let different systems and vendors work together.

children.title: RFC documents and IETF
children.definition: Requests for comments are the working documents of the Internet Engineering Task Force, and some become full standards after maturity levels.

children.title: W3C, ISO and IEEE
children.definition: W3C standardises web technologies, ISO standardises broad information technology and IEEE standardises local area networks.

children.title: Maturity levels of a standard
children.definition: Proposed standard, draft standard, Internet standard and historic or experimental status.

children.title: Why standards matter
children.definition: Interoperability, portability and the ability of any browser to talk to any server.

card.explanation: Internet standards are agreed specifications that let systems from different vendors work together. They begin as requests for comments, the working documents of the Internet Engineering Task Force. A specification moves through maturity levels: proposed standard, draft standard and then Internet standard, while some stay experimental or become historic. Other bodies matter too: W3C standardises web technologies, ISO covers information technology broadly, and IEEE standardises local area networks. The point of all of it is interoperability. Any browser can talk to any server because both follow the same written rules.
card.example: A phone from one maker loads a page hosted on another because HTTP and HTML are written down and agreed by everyone.

quiz.q: What is an RFC?
options: A request for comments, the working document of the IETF
quiz.why: Every Internet protocol is published as an RFC before it can become a standard.

quiz.q: Which organisation standardises web technologies such as HTML and CSS?
quiz.why: The World Wide Web Consortium publishes the specifications that browsers implement.

quiz.q: Which statement about Internet standards is NOT correct?
options: They let equipment from different vendors interoperate
A standard is final the moment it is first written
They pass through proposed and draft stages
quiz.why: Maturity levels exist so a specification is tested in practice before it becomes final.

quiz.q: Which maturity level comes after draft standard?
quiz.why: The sequence runs proposed, then draft, then Internet standard.

quiz.q: Why do standards matter most?
options: They give interoperability between products from different vendors
They reduce the number of protocols
They make equipment cheaper to manufacture
quiz.why: Interoperability is why a browser and a server written by different teams can communicate.

card.examTip: Define RFC, give the roles of IETF, W3C, ISO and IEEE, and list the maturity levels in order.

topics.title: Introduction to the World Wide Web
topics.definition: The web is an information system of linked hypertext documents accessed over the Internet.

children.title: Web page, website and hyperlinks
children.definition: A page is one document, a site is a collection of related pages and hyperlinks connect them.

children.title: Web browser and web server
children.definition: The browser requests and renders content while the server stores and delivers it.

children.title: Static versus dynamic pages
children.definition: Static pages are stored ready made, dynamic pages are generated for each request.

children.title: Web evolution: Web 1.0 to Web 3.0
children.definition: From read only pages to social and interactive applications to semantic and decentralised ideas.

card.explanation: The web is an information system of linked hypertext documents reached over the Internet. A web page is one document, a website is a collection of related pages, and hyperlinks connect them. The browser requests and renders content, while the web server stores it and sends it when asked. Pages may be static, stored ready made and sent unchanged, or dynamic, built for each request. The web has moved through three broad stages: read only pages, then social and interactive applications, then semantic and decentralised ideas.
card.example: A college notice page that never changes is static. The same site's results page, built when you enter a roll number, is dynamic.

quiz.q: What is the difference between a web page and a website?
options: A page is one document, a site is a collection of related pages
quiz.why: The site is the container and each page is a document inside it.

quiz.q: Which statement about static pages is NOT correct?
options: They are sent unchanged to every visitor
They are generated separately for each request
They suit content that rarely changes
quiz.why: Building a page for each request is what a dynamic page does.

quiz.q: What is the role of a web server?
options: To connect the user to the Internet
To display pages to the user
To store content and deliver it when requested
quiz.why: The server waits for requests, and the browser is what renders the response.

quiz.q: Which describes Web 2.0?
quiz.why: Web 2.0 is the stage where users create content as well as read it.

quiz.q: What connects one document to another on the web?
quiz.why: Hyperlinks are what make the web a web rather than a pile of documents.

card.examTip: Define web page, website and hyperlink, contrast static and dynamic pages, and name the three web stages.

topics.title: WWW Architecture
topics.definition: WWW architecture describes how browsers, servers and the network cooperate to deliver web content.

children.title: Client server model of the web
children.definition: The browser is the client, the web server is the server and HTTP carries the requests and responses.

children.title: Three tier architecture
children.definition: Presentation, application logic and data tiers separate the interface, business rules and storage.

children.title: Web server software and hosting
children.definition: Apache, Nginx and IIS serve content from a document root with configuration for virtual hosts.

children.title: Web caching and proxies
children.definition: Forward and reverse proxies plus content delivery networks reduce latency and server load.

card.explanation: Web architecture describes how browsers, servers and the network cooperate to deliver content. The web uses the client server model: the browser is the client and the web server is the server. HTTP carries the requests and responses between them. Larger applications add a three tier structure, with a presentation tier, an application logic tier and a data tier. Common server software includes Apache, Nginx and IIS, all serving files from a document root with configuration for virtual hosts. Caching shortens the journey: forward and reverse proxies and content delivery networks keep copies closer to the user.
card.example: A news site uses a CDN so that a reader in Chennai loads images from a nearby server rather than one in another country.

quiz.q: What are the three tiers of web architecture?
quiz.why: Separating interface, rules and storage lets each tier be changed alone.

quiz.q: Which is a web server?
quiz.why: Nginx, Apache and IIS are server software; the others are a browser, an operating system and a database.

quiz.q: Which statement about web architecture is NOT correct?
options: A CDN makes the origin server unnecessary
The browser acts as the client
A reverse proxy sits in front of the servers
quiz.why: A CDN caches copies, but the origin server still holds the authoritative content.

quiz.q: What is the document root?
options: The folder the server serves files from
quiz.why: A URL path is mapped to a file inside that directory on the server.

quiz.q: What does a forward proxy do?
options: Acts on behalf of clients, often for caching and filtering
quiz.why: It stands between users and the Internet, which lets an organisation cache and control traffic.

card.examTip: Draw the client server model, name the three tiers, two servers and two caching mechanisms.

topics.title: SMTP, POP3 and IMAP
topics.definition: Email is delivered by push protocols and retrieved by pull protocols.

children.title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP)
children.definition: Push protocol on port 25 that sends mail from client to server and between servers.

children.title: Post Office Protocol version 3 (POP3)
children.definition: Pull protocol on port 110 that downloads messages, usually deleting them from the server.

children.title: Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP)
children.definition: Port 143 protocol that keeps mail on the server, supports folders and synchronises across devices.

children.title: Email message format and MIME
children.definition: Headers plus body defined by RFC 822, with MIME allowing attachments and non-ASCII content.

card.explanation: Email is delivered by push protocols and retrieved by pull protocols. SMTP is the push protocol: it runs on port 25 and moves mail from a client to a server and between servers. POP3 is a pull protocol on port 110 that downloads messages and usually deletes them from the server. IMAP, on port 143, keeps the mail on the server, supports folders and synchronises across devices. A message itself has headers and a body defined by RFC 822, and MIME extends it so that attachments and non-ASCII content can travel.
card.example: Reading office mail on a phone and a laptop with the same folders is IMAP at work. POP3 would have emptied the server on the first device.

quiz.q: Which protocol sends mail from a client to a server?
quiz.why: SMTP pushes the message onward, which is why it is called a push protocol.

quiz.q: Which protocol keeps mail on the server and synchronises across devices?
quiz.why: IMAP manages folders on the server, so every device sees the same state.

quiz.q: Which statement about email protocols is NOT correct?
options: POP3 is the best choice for reading mail on several devices
quiz.why: POP3 downloads and often deletes, which leaves other devices without the messages.

quiz.q: What does MIME add to email?
options: Support for attachments and non-ASCII content
quiz.why: MIME extends the plain text format of RFC 822 with multipart bodies and encodings.

quiz.q: Which port does IMAP use?
quiz.why: Port 143 is the standard IMAP port, with 993 used for IMAP over TLS.

card.examTip: Compare SMTP, POP3 and IMAP with port numbers and one behaviour each, and mention MIME.

topics.title: File Transfer Protocol (FTP)
topics.definition: FTP transfers files between a client and a server using two separate connections.

children.title: Control and data connections
children.definition: The control connection on port 21 carries commands while the data connection carries the file.

children.title: Active and passive modes
children.definition: Active lets the server open the data connection to the client; passive lets the client open it, which works through firewalls.

children.title: FTP commands and replies
children.definition: USER, PASS, RETR, STOR, LIST and QUIT with three digit reply codes.

children.title: Secure alternatives
children.definition: SFTP over SSH and FTPS over TLS replace plain FTP for confidential transfers.

card.explanation: FTP moves files between a client and a server using two separate connections. The control connection on port 21 carries the commands, and a second data connection carries the file itself. In active mode the server opens the data connection back to the client, which firewalls often block. In passive mode the client opens the data connection instead, which works through most firewalls. The commands are simple: USER, PASS, RETR, STOR, LIST and QUIT, each answered with a three digit reply code. Because FTP sends everything in the clear, SFTP over SSH and FTPS over TLS are used where the transfer must stay private.
card.example: A designer uploads a site with an FTP client. When the client sits behind a firewall, switching to passive mode usually fixes a stalled transfer.

quiz.q: Which port carries FTP commands?
quiz.why: Port 21 is the control connection, while the data connection uses another port.

quiz.q: Which mode works better through a firewall?
quiz.why: Passive mode has the client open the data connection, which outbound rules usually allow.

quiz.q: Which statement about FTP is NOT correct?
options: FTP encrypts the data by default
quiz.why: Plain FTP sends credentials and files unencrypted, which is why SFTP and FTPS exist.

quiz.q: What does the FTP command LIST do?
options: Lists the files in the current directory
quiz.why: It returns a directory listing over the data connection.

quiz.q: What is FTPS?
quiz.why: FTPS adds TLS encryption to FTP, while SFTP runs over SSH instead.

card.examTip: Describe the two FTP connections, compare active and passive mode, and name two secure alternatives.

topics.title: Overview of HTTP and the Request Response Model
topics.definition: HTTP is the stateless request response protocol of the web.

children.title: Request message structure
children.definition: Request line with method and URL, headers, a blank line and an optional body.

children.title: Response message structure
children.definition: Status line, headers such as content type and length, a blank line and the body.

children.title: Methods and status codes
children.definition: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, HEAD and OPTIONS; 1xx to 5xx status classes.

children.title: Headers, content types and cookies
children.definition: Metadata such as Accept, User-Agent and Set-Cookie that shape caching, sessions and content negotiation.

children.title: Persistent connections and pipelining
children.definition: Keep alive lets many requests share one TCP connection, which lowers latency.

children.title: HTTPS
children.definition: HTTP over TLS encrypts traffic and verifies the server identity with certificates.

card.explanation: HTTP is the request response protocol of the web, and it is stateless: the server keeps no memory of earlier requests. A request has a request line with the method and URL, headers, a blank line and an optional body. A response has a status line, headers such as content type and length, a blank line and the body. The common methods are GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, HEAD and OPTIONS, and status codes fall into classes from 1xx to 5xx. Headers carry metadata, and cookies let a stateful session be built on a stateless protocol. Keep alive lets many requests share one TCP connection, and HTTPS puts the whole exchange inside TLS.
card.example: A 404 means the page was not found and a 500 means the server failed. Both are three digit codes in the status line.

quiz.q: What does HTTP status code 404 mean?
quiz.why: Codes in the 4xx class report a problem with the request, and 404 is the familiar one.

quiz.q: Which method asks the server for a resource without changing anything?
quiz.why: GET retrieves, while POST, PUT and DELETE are meant to change something.

quiz.q: Which statement about HTTP is NOT correct?
options: It is a request response protocol
A request has a request line, headers and an optional body
Cookies make the protocol stateful by themselves
quiz.why: HTTP stays stateless; cookies are data the client returns so a session can be rebuilt.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the Keep Alive header?
options: To reuse one TCP connection for several requests
quiz.why: Reusing the connection avoids the cost of a new handshake for every resource.

quiz.q: Which status class indicates a server error?
quiz.why: 5xx codes mean the server failed, while 4xx codes mean the request was at fault.

card.examTip: Sketch a request and a response, name five methods and the five status classes, and explain cookies and HTTPS.

topics.title: Generation of Dynamic Web Pages
topics.definition: Dynamic pages are built at request time on the server, on the client or on both.

children.title: Common Gateway Interface (CGI)
children.definition: An old standard in which the server starts a separate program for each request, which is simple but slow.

children.title: Server side scripting
children.definition: PHP, JSP, ASP.NET, Python and Node.js generate HTML on the server before it is sent.

children.title: Client side scripting
children.definition: JavaScript runs in the browser to update the page without a full reload.

children.title: Server side includes and templating
children.definition: Reusable fragments and templates are combined with data to build the final page.

card.explanation: Dynamic pages are built when the request arrives, on the server, on the client or on both. The oldest approach is the Common Gateway Interface, where the server starts a separate program for each request, which is simple but slow. Server side scripting is the usual answer now. PHP, JSP, ASP.NET, Python or Node.js builds the HTML on the server before it is sent. Client side scripting works the other way, with JavaScript in the browser updating the page without a full reload. Templating and server side includes tie it together, combining reusable fragments with data to produce the final page.
card.example: A weather page built by PHP on the server shows fresh data on every load. The same page can then update one number with JavaScript, without reloading.

quiz.q: What is the main drawback of CGI?
options: A new process starts for every request, which is slow
quiz.why: Process creation costs time and memory, so CGI scales poorly.

quiz.q: Which runs on the server and is invisible to the user?
quiz.why: The server executes PHP and sends only the resulting HTML, so the source never reaches the browser.

quiz.q: Which statement about dynamic pages is NOT correct?
options: Every dynamic page needs a database
They can be built on the server
They can be built in the browser
quiz.why: A page can be dynamic from a clock, a file or an API, not only from a database.

quiz.q: What does client side scripting avoid?
quiz.why: JavaScript updates part of the page, so the user does not wait for a new document.

quiz.q: Which of these is a server side technology?
quiz.why: ASP.NET, PHP, JSP and Node.js all run on the server before the response is sent.

card.examTip: Define a dynamic page, describe CGI and its drawback, and contrast server side and client side scripting.

modules.title: HTML and CSS for User Interface Design

topics.title: Introduction to HTML and HTML5
topics.definition: HTML is the markup language that gives structure and meaning to web content.

children.title: Document structure
children.definition: DOCTYPE, html, head with title and meta tags, and body holding the visible content.

children.title: Tags, elements and attributes
children.definition: Elements are written with opening and closing tags and configured by attributes such as id, class and src.

children.title: HTML5 semantic elements
children.definition: header, nav, main, section, article, aside, figure and footer describe the role of each part.

children.title: HTML5 features
children.definition: Native audio and video, canvas, SVG, local storage, web workers and better form input types.

children.title: Headings and paragraph elements
children.definition: h1 to h6 for hierarchy and p, br and hr for text blocks and breaks.

card.explanation: HTML is the markup language that gives structure and meaning to web content. A document opens with a DOCTYPE, then an html element containing a head and a body. The head holds the title and meta tags, and the body holds everything the reader sees. Elements are written with an opening tag, content and a closing tag, and attributes such as id, class and src configure them. HTML5 added semantic elements: header, nav, main, section, article, aside, figure and footer each say what their part is. It also added native audio and video, canvas, SVG, local storage, web workers and better form inputs.
card.example: Writing nav around the menu links tells a screen reader that this block is navigation, not ordinary text.

quiz.q: Which element holds the visible content of a page?
quiz.why: The head carries metadata, and everything the reader sees sits in the body.

quiz.q: Which HTML5 element marks the main navigation block?
quiz.why: Semantic elements describe the role of a block, which helps browsers and assistive tools.

quiz.q: Which statement about HTML is NOT correct?
options: The DOCTYPE declares the document type
HTML5 removed every formatting element such as b and i
Elements usually have opening and closing tags
Attributes such as id and class configure elements
quiz.why: Elements such as b and i still exist, though CSS is the preferred way to style text.

quiz.q: Which HTML5 feature draws graphics with script?
quiz.why: The canvas element gives a drawing surface that JavaScript can paint on.

quiz.q: What does a meta tag do?
options: Carries metadata such as character set and viewport
quiz.why: Meta tags describe the document itself rather than displaying content.

card.examTip: Sketch the document skeleton, name four semantic elements and four HTML5 features.

topics.title: Formatting, Fonts, Comments and Backgrounds
topics.definition: Formatting elements control the look of text while comments document the code.

children.title: Text formatting elements
children.definition: b, i, u, strong, em, sub, sup, mark, small and del change the appearance or meaning of text.

children.title: Fonts and colours
children.definition: The font tag is obsolete; modern pages use CSS font-family, size and colour instead.

children.title: Commenting code
children.definition: Comments are written between the symbols for less-than, exclamation, two dashes and their mirror image, and are ignored by the browser.

children.title: Backgrounds
children.definition: Background colour and images were set with attributes in old HTML and are set with CSS today.

card.explanation: Formatting elements change the appearance or the meaning of text. The b and i elements make text bold and italic. The strong and em elements carry importance and emphasis, which matters to screen readers. Other elements include u, sub, sup, mark, small and del. Comments let a developer leave notes in the file, and the browser ignores them completely. Old HTML set fonts and colours with the font tag and with attributes on the body element. Modern pages use CSS instead, with font-family, size and colour, which keeps presentation separate from content.
card.example: Using strong instead of b means a screen reader can stress the word rather than ignore the styling.

quiz.q: Which element indicates importance rather than bold styling?
quiz.why: strong carries meaning, while b only changes the appearance.

quiz.q: What happens to an HTML comment in the browser?
options: It is shown in small text
It is ignored and never rendered
It is printed at the top of the page
quiz.why: Comments exist for the people reading the source, not for the reader of the page.

quiz.q: Which statement about formatting is NOT correct?
options: sup raises text above the line
The font tag is the recommended way to set type
CSS is preferred for fonts and colours
quiz.why: The font element is obsolete, and CSS replaced it.

quiz.q: Which element marks text that has been deleted?
quiz.why: del carries the meaning of removal, which is why it suits edit histories.

quiz.q: How is text coloured in a modern page?
quiz.why: CSS separates presentation from content, so one change updates every page.

card.examTip: List four formatting elements, explain strong versus b, and say why CSS replaced the font tag.

topics.title: Anchors, Hyperlinks and Images
topics.definition: Links connect documents and images embed pictures in a page.

children.title: Anchor tag and href
children.definition: The a element creates a link using href, which may point to a page, a section, an email address or a file.

children.title: Types of hyperlinks
children.definition: Internal links within a site, external links to other sites, and fragment links to a section of the same page.

children.title: Target attribute and link behaviour
children.definition: target makes a link open in a new tab or a named frame.

children.title: Image tag, alt text and formats
children.definition: The img element uses src and alt with JPEG, PNG, GIF, SVG and WebP formats for different needs.

children.title: Image maps and figure captions
children.definition: Map regions of one image to different links and use figure with figcaption for captions.

card.explanation: The a element creates a link, and its href attribute says where the link goes. That destination may be another page, a section of the same page, an email address or a file to download. Links are internal when they stay inside the site and external when they leave it. A fragment link jumps to an element with a matching id. The target attribute decides where the result opens, such as in a new tab. Images use the img element with src for the file and alt for the text alternative. Formats differ in purpose: JPEG suits photographs and PNG suits sharp graphics. GIF suits simple animation, SVG suits scalable drawings and WebP gives smaller files.
card.example: An image with a missing alt attribute leaves a screen reader with nothing to announce. A short description fixes that.

quiz.q: Which attribute holds the destination of a link?
quiz.why: href names the target resource, while src is used for embedded files such as images.

quiz.q: What is a fragment link?
options: A link that opens a file
A link to a section of the same page using an id
quiz.why: The URL ends with a hash and the element id, so the browser scrolls to that place.

quiz.q: Which statement about images is NOT correct?
options: WebP usually produces smaller files than JPEG
quiz.why: SVG is vector based, so it stays sharp at any size.

quiz.q: Which attribute opens a link in a new tab?
quiz.why: Setting target makes the browser open the result in a new tab or a named frame.

quiz.q: Which image format suits a logo that must scale?
quiz.why: SVG describes shapes rather than pixels, so it scales without losing sharpness.

card.examTip: Write an anchor tag with href and target, list three link types, and compare four image formats.

topics.title: Lists, Tables and Frames
topics.definition: Lists group items, tables arrange data in rows and columns and frames embed or split content.

children.title: Ordered and unordered lists
children.definition: ol numbers items and ul marks them with bullets, with li marking each item and nested lists allowed.

children.title: Definition lists
children.definition: dl with dt for the term and dd for its description.

children.title: Creating tables
children.definition: table, caption, thead, tbody, tr, th and td give rows, headers and cells.

children.title: Rowspan and colspan plus nested tables
children.definition: Cells can span several rows or columns, and tables can be nested inside cells.

children.title: Framesets and iframes
children.definition: Framesets split a window into panes and are obsolete; iframe embeds another document inside a page.

card.explanation: Lists group related items, and there are three kinds. An ordered list numbers its items and an unordered list marks them with bullets. A definition list pairs a term with its description. Each item is written with li, and lists may be nested inside one another. Tables arrange data in rows and columns using table, tr, th and td, with caption, thead and tbody giving structure. A cell can span several rows or columns with rowspan and colspan. Framesets once split a window into panes but are obsolete now, while the iframe element embeds another document inside a page.
card.example: A timetable needs a table with th for the days and td for each subject. A list would lose the row and column structure.

quiz.q: Which list pairs a term with its description?
quiz.why: A definition list uses dl with dt for the term and dd for the description.

quiz.q: Which element marks a header cell in a table?
quiz.why: th marks a header cell and td an ordinary data cell, and browsers style them differently.

quiz.q: Which statement about tables is NOT correct?
options: Tables should be used to lay out a whole page
colspan makes a cell span columns
rowspan makes a cell span rows
quiz.why: Layout is a CSS job, and tables are meant for data with rows and columns.

quiz.q: Which element embeds another document inside a page?
quiz.why: The iframe element is still supported, while framesets were removed from HTML5.

quiz.q: Which element gives a table a title?
quiz.why: caption is placed inside the table element and describes what the table shows.

card.examTip: Name the three list types with their tags, the table tags, and explain rowspan, colspan and iframe.

topics.title: HTML Forms
topics.definition: Forms collect user input and submit it to a server for processing.

children.title: Form element and action
children.definition: The form tag names the processing URL with action and the sending method with method, usually GET or POST.

children.title: Input types
children.definition: text, password, email, number, date, radio, checkbox, file, hidden, submit and reset with attributes name, value and placeholder.

children.title: Select, option, textarea and button
children.definition: Drop down lists, multi-line text and buttons with caption or image.

children.title: Labels, fieldsets and accessibility
children.definition: label ties text to a control and fieldset with legend groups related controls.

children.title: Client side validation attributes
children.definition: required, pattern, min, max and maxlength check input before submission, with HTML5 validation messages.

card.explanation: A form collects user input and sends it to a server for processing. The form element names the processing URL with action and the sending method with method, usually GET or POST. Inside it, the input element covers many types: text, password, email, number, date, radio, checkbox, file, hidden, submit and reset. Drop down lists use select with option, longer text uses textarea, and button gives a clickable control. Every control should have a name, because that is what the server reads. Labels and fieldsets improve accessibility, and attributes such as required, pattern, min and max validate input in the browser before submission.
card.example: A signup form with required on the email field stops an empty submission before any request reaches the server.

quiz.q: Which attribute names the script that will process a form?
quiz.why: action gives the destination URL, while method says how the data will be sent.

quiz.q: When should POST be used instead of GET?
options: For sensitive or large data, sent in the request body
quiz.why: GET puts data in the URL, which is visible and limited in size.

quiz.q: Which statement about forms is NOT correct?
options: select creates a drop down list
Client side validation is enough on its own
A control needs a name to be submitted
quiz.why: Browser validation can be bypassed, so the server must validate as well.

quiz.q: Which element ties a caption to a control?
quiz.why: A label with a for attribute makes the caption clickable and helps screen readers.

quiz.q: Which input type shows dots instead of characters?
quiz.why: The password type masks what is typed, though it does not encrypt the value sent.

card.examTip: Write a form tag with action and method, list five input types, and explain labels and validation.

topics.title: Cascading Style Sheets: Need, Syntax and Types
topics.definition: CSS separates presentation from content and controls layout, colour and typography.

children.title: Why CSS is needed
children.definition: Consistency across pages, easier maintenance, smaller HTML and separation of concerns.

children.title: Syntax and structure
children.definition: A rule has a selector and a declaration block of property value pairs, with comments and units.

children.title: Inline styles
children.definition: Applied with the style attribute on one element only, which has the highest priority but cannot be reused.

children.title: Embedded (internal) style sheets
children.definition: Written in a style element in the head, which applies to one page.

children.title: Linking external style sheets
children.definition: The link element with rel stylesheet shares one CSS file across an entire site.

children.title: Cascade, specificity and inheritance
children.definition: Later, more specific rules win, and inheritable properties pass from parent to child.

card.explanation: CSS separates presentation from content and controls layout, colour and typography. It is needed because one stylesheet keeps a whole site consistent, makes maintenance easier and keeps HTML smaller. A rule has a selector and a declaration block of property value pairs, each ending with a semicolon. There are three ways to apply it. An inline style goes in the style attribute of one element and has the highest priority. An embedded sheet sits in a style element in the head and applies to one page. An external sheet is linked with the link element, and one file then styles an entire site.
card.example: Changing a colour in one linked stylesheet updates every page at once. Copying that change into fifty files would take hours.

quiz.q: Which type of stylesheet affects an entire site?
quiz.why: One external file is linked from every page, so a single edit updates them all.

quiz.q: What are the two parts of a CSS rule?
options: A selector and a declaration block
quiz.why: The selector chooses the elements and the declarations say what to change.

quiz.q: Which statement about CSS is NOT correct?
options: More specific selectors override less specific ones
Some properties are inherited from parent to child
External styles always override inline styles
Inline styles have the highest priority
quiz.why: Inline styles win over external ones, which is why they are used sparingly.

quiz.q: Which element links an external stylesheet?
quiz.why: The link element with rel stylesheet and an href points to the CSS file.

quiz.q: Why is CSS preferred over formatting tags?
options: It keeps presentation separate from content
quiz.why: Separation means the look can change without touching the structure or the text.

card.examTip: Explain why CSS is needed, write a rule, and compare inline, embedded and external stylesheets.

topics.title: CSS Text, Backgrounds, Box Model and Positioning
topics.definition: CSS controls typography, colour, spacing and where each element appears.

children.title: Text manipulation
children.definition: font-family, font-size, font-weight, line-height, letter-spacing, text-align and text-decoration.

children.title: Backgrounds and borders
children.definition: Background colour, gradients or images, with border radius and box shadow for styling.

children.title: Margins and padding
children.definition: Margin is space outside the border and padding is space inside it; the box model is content, padding, border and margin.

children.title: Width, height and overflow
children.definition: Box sizing decides whether padding is included in the width, and overflow decides what happens to excess content.

children.title: Positioning
children.definition: Static, relative, absolute, fixed and sticky positioning, with z-index for stacking order.

children.title: Float, flexbox and grid
children.definition: Floats for wrapping text, flexbox for one dimensional layouts and grid for two dimensional layouts.

children.title: Responsive design and media queries
children.definition: Percentages, flexible units and media queries adapt one layout to phones, tablets and desktops.

card.explanation: CSS controls typography, colour, spacing and the position of every element. Text is shaped with font-family, font-size, font-weight, line-height, letter-spacing, text-align and text-decoration. Backgrounds take a colour, a gradient or an image, and borders get rounded corners and shadows. The box model is the key idea: content, padding, border and margin. Box-sizing decides whether padding counts towards the declared width. Position can be static, relative, absolute, fixed or sticky, with z-index setting the stacking order. Layout uses floats for wrapping text, flexbox for one dimension and grid for two. Media queries adapt the layout to smaller screens.
card.example: A card with 20 pixels of padding and a 1 pixel border is 42 pixels wider than its content unless box-sizing is set to border-box.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the box model from the inside out?
quiz.why: Padding is inside the border, and margin is the space outside it.

quiz.q: Which positioning value keeps an element in place while the page scrolls?
quiz.why: Fixed positioning removes the element from the flow and pins it to the viewport.

quiz.q: Which statement about layout is NOT correct?
options: Flexbox handles one dimension at a time
Grid handles rows and columns together
Floats are the best tool for a full page layout
quiz.why: Floats suit wrapping text around an image, while flexbox and grid handle real layouts.

quiz.q: What does box-sizing border-box do?
options: Includes padding and border in the declared width
quiz.why: Without it, padding and border are added on top of the width you set.

quiz.q: What does z-index control?
options: The stacking order of overlapping elements
quiz.why: A higher z-index draws an element in front of one with a lower value.

card.examTip: Draw the box model, list the five position values, and compare float, flexbox and grid.

topics.title: JavaScript: Introduction and Core Features
topics.definition: JavaScript is the scripting language of the browser that makes pages interactive and can also run on servers.

children.title: Where JavaScript runs
children.definition: In the browser engine, inside HTML with the script tag, in external files and on the server through Node.js.

children.title: Core features
children.definition: Interpreted, dynamically typed, object based, event driven and single threaded with an event loop.

children.title: Advantages and limitations
children.definition: Fast client side validation and rich interfaces, but browser differences and client side security limits.

children.title: Adding JavaScript to a page
children.definition: Inline handlers, the script element inside head or body, and external .js files with defer or async.

card.explanation: JavaScript is the scripting language of the browser, and it is what makes a page interactive. It can also run outside the browser nowadays, on a server through Node.js. The language is interpreted, dynamically typed and object based, and it is event driven with a single thread and an event loop. Code reaches a page in three ways: inline handlers, a script element, or an external file. External files are preferred, and defer or async control when the code runs. Its strengths are instant validation and rich interfaces. Its limits are browser differences and the fact that the user can see the code.
card.example: A page that checks a mobile number as you type is using JavaScript. The same check could run on the server, but not instantly.

quiz.q: Where can JavaScript run besides the browser?
quiz.why: Node.js runs the same language outside the browser, which is why it is used for servers.

quiz.q: What does defer do on a script tag?
options: Runs the script after the document is parsed
quiz.why: Deferred scripts run in order once the page structure exists, so they can find elements.

quiz.q: Which statement about JavaScript is NOT correct?
options: It is the same language as Java
It uses a single thread with an event loop
quiz.why: The shared name is a historical accident; the two languages are quite different.

quiz.q: Which is a limitation of client side JavaScript?
options: The user can see and modify the code
quiz.why: Anything that runs in the browser is under the user's control, so the server must recheck.

quiz.q: What is the preferred way to add JavaScript to a page?
quiz.why: An external file can be cached, reused across pages and kept out of the markup.

card.examTip: Say where JavaScript runs, list its core features, the three ways to include it, and one limit.

topics.title: Data Types, Variables, Operators and Statements
topics.definition: JavaScript variables hold values of primitive or object types, and expressions are built with operators and statements.

children.title: Data types
children.definition: Primitive types string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol, plus object types including arrays and functions.

children.title: Variables: var, let and const
children.definition: var is function scoped and hoisted, let is block scoped and const cannot be reassigned.

children.title: Operators and expressions
children.definition: Arithmetic, comparison with == and ===, logical, assignment, ternary and typeof operators.

children.title: Statements and control flow
children.definition: if, else, switch, for, while, do while, for of, for in, break, continue and try catch finally.

children.title: Type conversion and coercion
children.definition: Implicit conversion by operators and explicit conversion with Number, String and Boolean.

card.explanation: JavaScript values are either primitive or objects. The primitive types are string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol, and everything else, including arrays and functions, is an object. Variables are declared with var, let or const, and the difference matters. var is function scoped and hoisted, let is block scoped, and const cannot be reassigned. Operators build expressions out of values: arithmetic, comparison, logical, assignment, ternary and typeof. Comparison has a trap, because the double equals operator converts types before comparing while the triple equals does not. Control flow uses if, else, switch, for, while, do while, for of and for in, with break, continue and try catch finally.
card.example: The expression 5 == '5' is true, but 5 === '5' is false. That difference causes a surprising number of bugs.

quiz.q: What is the difference between let and var?
options: let is block scoped, var is function scoped and hoisted
quiz.why: Block scoping keeps a variable inside the braces where it was declared, which avoids surprises.

quiz.q: Which of these is a primitive type?
quiz.why: Arrays, objects and functions are object types, while symbol is one of the primitives.

quiz.q: Which statement about JavaScript is NOT correct?
options: The triple equals operator compares without converting types
undefined and null are the same value
const prevents reassignment of the binding
typeof returns the type of a value
quiz.why: undefined means a variable has no value, while null is a value meaning no object.

quiz.q: What does the ternary operator do?
options: Chooses one of two values based on a condition
quiz.why: It is a compact form of if and else that produces a value.

quiz.q: Which loop iterates over the values of an array?
quiz.why: for of gives the values, while for in walks the property names of an object.

card.examTip: List the primitive types, compare var, let and const, explain == versus ===, and name four loops.

topics.title: Functions
topics.definition: A function is a reusable block of code that may take parameters and return a value.

children.title: Function declaration and expression
children.definition: Declarations are hoisted while function expressions are assigned to variables.

children.title: Parameters, arguments and return
children.definition: Parameters receive values, arguments holds them, and return sends a value back with undefined as the default.

children.title: Scope, closures and hoisting
children.definition: A closure remembers the variables of the function that created it.

children.title: Arrow functions and callbacks
children.definition: Shorter syntax with lexical this, commonly used as callbacks and event handlers.

children.title: Rest, spread and default parameters
children.definition: Modern syntax for flexible argument lists and copying or expanding arrays and objects.

card.explanation: A function is a reusable block of code that may take parameters and return a value. A function declaration is hoisted, so it can be called before it appears in the file. A function expression assigned to a variable cannot be called that way. Parameters receive the arguments, the arguments object holds them all, and return sends a value back, with undefined as the default. Scope decides what a function can see. A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the one that created it. Arrow functions give shorter syntax with lexical this, so they are common as callbacks. Modern syntax adds rest, spread and default parameters.
card.example: A counter built with a closure keeps its own count. Two counters made the same way never share that number.

quiz.q: What is a closure?
options: A function that remembers the variables of the function that created it
A way to end a function
quiz.why: The inner function keeps a reference to the outer scope, so the value survives the call.

quiz.q: What does a function return if there is no return statement?
quiz.why: Every function returns something, and without a return the value is undefined.

quiz.q: Which statement about functions is NOT correct?
options: A function expression can be stored in a variable
Parameters and scope are the same thing
quiz.why: Parameters are the names receiving arguments, while scope is about what is visible inside.

quiz.q: What does the rest parameter do?
options: Collects the remaining arguments into an array
quiz.why: It lets a function accept any number of arguments without naming them all.

quiz.q: Why is an arrow function often used as a callback?
options: It keeps the surrounding this value instead of rebinding it
quiz.why: Lexical this avoids the old workaround of storing this in another variable.

card.examTip: Compare declaration and expression, define closure and arrow function, and explain return, rest and spread.

topics.title: Objects, Arrays, Date and Math
topics.definition: JavaScript provides built-in objects for structured data, dates and mathematical operations.

children.title: Objects and properties
children.definition: Objects store key value pairs; properties and methods are accessed with a dot or brackets.

children.title: Arrays and their methods
children.definition: Arrays are ordered collections with push, pop, shift, unshift, slice, splice, map, filter, reduce, sort and forEach.

children.title: Strings and their methods
children.definition: length, charAt, indexOf, substring, slice, split, replace, toUpperCase and trim.

children.title: Date object
children.definition: Creates and manipulates dates with getFullYear, getMonth, getTime and parsing of date strings.

children.title: Math object
children.definition: Math.round, floor, ceil, abs, pow, sqrt, random, min and max.

children.title: Regular expressions
children.definition: Patterns used with test, match, replace and split for validation and searching.

card.explanation: JavaScript supplies built-in objects for structured data, dates and mathematics. An object stores key value pairs, and its properties and methods are reached with a dot or with square brackets. An array is an ordered collection with two families of methods. push, pop, shift, unshift and splice change the array itself. slice, map, filter and reduce return something new. Strings have their own methods, including length, indexOf, slice, split, replace and trim. The Date object handles dates and times, and the Math object supplies round, floor, ceil, abs, pow, sqrt, random, min and max. Regular expressions add pattern matching through test, match, replace and split.
card.example: Filtering a list of marks above 60 is one line with filter. Sorting needs a compare function, because sort compares strings by default.

quiz.q: Which array method returns a new array instead of changing the original?
quiz.why: map, filter and slice leave the original alone, which makes them safer to use.

quiz.q: How are object properties accessed?
options: With a dot or with square brackets
quiz.why: Bracket notation also allows a property name held in a variable.

quiz.q: Which statement about built-in objects is NOT correct?
options: Math.random returns a number below one
Date objects can be compared by subtraction
split joins array elements into a string
quiz.why: split breaks a string into an array, while join does the opposite.

quiz.q: Which Math method rounds down to the nearest integer?
quiz.why: floor rounds down, ceil rounds up and round goes to the nearest.

quiz.q: Which method tests whether a string matches a pattern?
quiz.why: A regular expression's test method returns true or false, which suits validation.

card.examTip: List four array methods of each family, four string methods, and the roles of Date, Math and regex.

topics.title: Document Object Model (DOM)
topics.definition: The DOM is a tree representation of the page that JavaScript can read and modify.

children.title: DOM tree and nodes
children.definition: Elements, attributes and text form a hierarchy under the document node.

children.title: Selecting elements
children.definition: getElementById, getElementsByClassName, getElementsByTagName, querySelector and querySelectorAll.

children.title: Changing content and attributes
children.definition: innerHTML, textContent, setAttribute, classList, and style manipulation.

children.title: Creating and removing elements
children.definition: createElement, appendChild, insertBefore, removeChild and cloneNode for dynamic page updates.

children.title: Traversing the DOM
children.definition: parentNode, children, firstElementChild, nextElementSibling and closest.

card.explanation: The DOM is a tree representation of the page that JavaScript can read and change. Elements, attributes and text become nodes in a hierarchy under the document node. Elements are found with getElementById, getElementsByClassName, getElementsByTagName, querySelector and querySelectorAll. Content is then changed with innerHTML, textContent and setAttribute, while classList and style handle appearance. New nodes are built with createElement and placed with appendChild or insertBefore, and removed with removeChild. Traversal moves around the tree using parentNode, children, firstElementChild, nextElementSibling and closest.
card.example: A shopping list app adds an item by creating an li element, setting its text and appending it to the ul.

quiz.q: Which method returns the first element matching a CSS selector?
quiz.why: querySelector takes any CSS selector and returns the first match, or null.

quiz.q: Which property should be used to insert plain text safely?
quiz.why: textContent treats the value as text, so it cannot inject markup the way innerHTML can.

quiz.q: Which statement about the DOM is NOT correct?
options: The DOM is the same thing as the HTML source file
The DOM is a tree of nodes
appendChild attaches a node to a parent
quiz.why: The DOM is the live object the browser builds from the source, and script can change it.

quiz.q: Which method removes a node from its parent?
quiz.why: removeChild is called on the parent and takes the node to be removed.

quiz.q: What does closest do?
options: Walks up to the nearest ancestor matching a selector
quiz.why: It starts at the element and searches upwards, which is handy in event handlers.

card.examTip: Explain the DOM tree, list three selection methods, three change methods and three traversal properties.

topics.title: Event Handling
topics.definition: Event handling lets the page respond to user actions such as clicks, typing and scrolling.

children.title: Event and event object
children.definition: The event object carries the type, target, coordinates, key and modifiers.

children.title: Event handlers and listeners
children.definition: Inline handlers, properties such as onclick and addEventListener with options.

children.title: Event flow: capture, target and bubble
children.definition: Events travel down to the target and bubble back up, and stopPropagation stops the journey.

children.title: Event delegation
children.definition: One listener on a parent handles events from many children, which is efficient for lists.

children.title: Common events
children.definition: click, dblclick, mouseover, keydown, keyup, change, input, submit, load, scroll and touch events.

children.title: Form events and validation
children.definition: preventDefault is used to stop submission while custom validation runs.

card.explanation: Event handling lets a page respond to clicks, typing, scrolling and the rest. The browser passes an event object that carries the type, the target, the coordinates, the key pressed and any modifier keys. Handlers can be attached as an inline attribute, a property, or with addEventListener. addEventListener is preferred, because several listeners can then coexist. Events travel in three phases: capture down to the target, the target itself, then bubble back up. Calling stopPropagation ends that journey. Event delegation puts one listener on a parent and lets it handle events from many children. Form work often calls preventDefault to stop submission while validation runs.
card.example: One listener on a table can handle clicks on any row. Adding a listener to every row would waste memory and break for new rows.

quiz.q: Why is addEventListener preferred over onclick?
options: It is the only one that fires
Several listeners can be attached and removed cleanly
quiz.why: A property holds one handler at a time, while listeners accumulate and can be removed.

quiz.q: What is event delegation?
options: One listener on a parent handling events from many children
Passing an event to the server
quiz.why: Events bubble up, so the parent can inspect the target and act accordingly.

quiz.q: Which statement about events is NOT correct?
options: Bubbling happens before the capture phase
The event object carries the target
Events bubble back up the tree
quiz.why: Capture runs first on the way down, then the target, then bubbling on the way up.

quiz.q: Which event fires while a user types in a field?
quiz.why: input fires on every change to the value, which suits live validation.

quiz.q: What does stopPropagation do?
options: Stops the event travelling further through the tree
quiz.why: It halts capture and bubbling, while preventDefault stops the browser's own action.

card.examTip: Name three ways to attach a handler, the three event phases, and explain delegation and preventDefault.

topics.title: Controlling Windows, Frames and Documents
topics.definition: JavaScript can open, resize, move and close windows and can access frames and documents.

children.title: Window object
children.definition: open, close, alert, confirm, prompt, moveTo, resizeTo, setTimeout and setInterval.

children.title: Navigator, screen, history and location
children.definition: Browser information, display size, browsing history and the current URL, with location.href performing redirection.

children.title: Frames and iframes
children.definition: Frame collections and accessing the document of a same origin frame.

children.title: Timers and animation
children.definition: setTimeout and setInterval drive repeated updates and simple animations.

card.explanation: The window object is the top of the browser object model, and it can open, close, move and resize windows. It also supplies the dialogs alert, confirm and prompt, and the timers setTimeout and setInterval. Around it sit other useful objects: navigator describes the browser, screen the display, history the visited pages and location the current URL. Assigning to location.href redirects the browser to a new page. Frames and iframes are reachable as collections. A script may reach into the document of a frame from the same origin. Timers are what drive repeated updates and simple animation.
card.example: A page that asks for confirmation before deleting uses confirm. A banner that changes every five seconds uses setInterval.

quiz.q: Which object holds the current URL?
quiz.why: location exposes the URL, and assigning to its href navigates somewhere else.

quiz.q: What is the difference between setTimeout and setInterval?
options: setTimeout runs once after a delay, setInterval repeats
quiz.why: setTimeout fires once, while setInterval keeps firing until it is cleared.

quiz.q: Which statement about windows is NOT correct?
options: Scripts may freely read any frame from any site
quiz.why: The same origin policy blocks access to documents from a different origin.

quiz.q: Which object describes the display size?
quiz.why: screen reports the display, while navigator reports the browser itself.

quiz.q: What does history.back do?
options: Goes to the previous page in the session history
quiz.why: The history object lets scripts move backwards and forwards through visited pages.

card.examTip: List five window methods, describe navigator, screen, history and location, and give the same origin rule.

topics.title: Form Handling and Validation in JavaScript
topics.definition: Forms are validated in the browser before submission to save server work and give instant feedback.

children.title: Accessing form elements
children.definition: document.forms, element names and values, checkbox and radio checked states.

children.title: Validation techniques
children.definition: Checking empty fields, lengths, patterns with regular expressions and numeric ranges.

children.title: Validation events and error display
children.definition: onsubmit, onblur and oninput with error messages placed near fields.

children.title: Advantages and limits of client side validation
children.definition: Fast feedback, but it can be bypassed, so server side validation is still required.

card.explanation: Forms are checked in the browser before submission, which saves the server work and gives the user instant feedback. A script reaches the controls through document.forms, element names or a selector. It then reads value, checked or the selected options. Validation checks the usual things: empty fields, lengths, patterns with regular expressions and numeric ranges. The checks are wired to events such as onsubmit, onblur and oninput, and error messages are placed next to the field that failed. Client side validation is fast and helpful, but it can be bypassed, so the server must validate every value again.
card.example: A form that checks the PIN code with a regular expression can warn about the format the moment the user leaves the field.

quiz.q: Why is client side validation still not enough?
options: It can be bypassed, so the server must check again
quiz.why: Anything in the browser is under the user's control, including the checks themselves.

quiz.q: Which event fires when a field loses focus?
quiz.why: onblur is the usual place to validate one field as soon as the user leaves it.

quiz.q: Which statement about form validation is NOT correct?
options: Values are read with the value property
Regular expressions can test a pattern
Error messages belong near the field
Server validation is optional if the browser checks
quiz.why: Server side validation is mandatory, because the browser's checks can be turned off.

quiz.q: How is the state of a checkbox read?
quiz.why: checked is a boolean, while value is the text sent when the box is ticked.

quiz.q: What does preventDefault do in a submit handler?
options: Stops the form submitting so the script can decide
quiz.why: The handler can then allow submission only if every check passes.

card.examTip: Describe reading form values, name three checks and three events, and say why server validation is required.

topics.title: Browser and Media Management
topics.definition: Browsers expose objects that let scripts manage windows, navigation and media content.

children.title: Browser object model
children.definition: window, document, navigator, screen, history and location together form the BOM.

children.title: Cookies and web storage
children.definition: Cookies carry small data with every request while localStorage and sessionStorage keep data in the browser only.

children.title: Handling images, audio and video
children.definition: The image objects, audio and video elements with play, pause, currentTime and volume control.

children.title: Canvas and SVG
children.definition: Canvas draws pixels through the 2D context while SVG describes vector graphics as XML.

children.title: Geolocation and device APIs
children.definition: The geolocation API, drag and drop, and the file reader API extend browser behaviour.

card.explanation: The browser object model gathers the objects the browser exposes: window, document, navigator, screen, history and location. Storage comes in two flavours. Cookies are small pieces of data sent with every request. localStorage and sessionStorage keep data in the browser only. Media is handled by elements and objects too. Images, audio and video can be played, paused, moved with currentTime and set to a volume. Graphics come in two styles: canvas draws pixels through a two dimensional context, while SVG describes vector shapes as XML. Beyond that, geolocation, drag and drop and the file reader API extend what a page can do.
card.example: A quiz site keeps unfinished answers in localStorage so a student can close the tab and return to them later.

quiz.q: What is the difference between cookies and localStorage?
options: Cookies are sent with every request, localStorage stays in the browser
quiz.why: Cookies travel to the server each time, while web storage never leaves the browser.

quiz.q: Which draws vector graphics as XML?
quiz.why: SVG describes shapes that stay sharp, while canvas paints pixels that are then fixed.

quiz.q: Which statement about browser storage is NOT correct?
options: Web storage data is sent to the server with each request
sessionStorage is cleared when the tab closes
localStorage persists until it is cleared
quiz.why: Avoiding that round trip is the point of web storage, which is why it suits larger data.

quiz.q: Which API reports the user's position?
quiz.why: Geolocation asks permission and then returns coordinates to the page.

quiz.q: Which collection of objects makes up the BOM?
options: window, document, navigator, screen, history and location
quiz.why: These objects describe the browser and the page rather than the HTML tags.

card.examTip: Name the BOM objects, compare cookies with web storage, and describe canvas, SVG and media control.

topics.title: Classes, Constructors and Object Orientation in JavaScript
topics.definition: Modern JavaScript provides class syntax over a prototype based object model.

children.title: Object constructors
children.definition: A constructor function initialises objects with this and new, and methods are placed on the prototype.

children.title: Prototypes and the prototype chain
children.definition: Objects inherit properties through links up the chain to Object.prototype.

children.title: Encapsulation with closures and private fields
children.definition: Data privacy is achieved with closures or the hash prefix private fields and static members.

children.title: ES6 class syntax
children.definition: class with constructor, methods, getters and setters is syntactic sugar over prototypes.

children.title: Inheritance: subclasses and superclasses
children.definition: extends creates a subclass and super calls the parent constructor or method.

children.title: Polymorphism and method overriding
children.definition: A subclass may replace a parent method, and the most derived version is called.

card.explanation: JavaScript objects are built on prototypes, and modern class syntax sits on top of that foundation. The older way uses a constructor function called with new. Inside it, this refers to the new object and shared methods go on the prototype. Every object links up a prototype chain to Object.prototype, and that chain is how properties are inherited. Encapsulation is achieved with closures or with private fields written with a hash prefix. The class keyword gives a cleaner syntax with a constructor, methods, getters and setters, and static members. Inheritance uses extends and super, and a subclass may override a parent method, with the most derived version being called.
card.example: A Student class extends Person. Calling super in the constructor sets the name, and the subclass adds a roll number.

quiz.q: What does the new keyword do?
options: Creates an object and calls the constructor with this bound to it
quiz.why: new makes a fresh object, sets its prototype and returns it from the constructor.

quiz.q: How is inheritance written with class syntax?
quiz.why: extends creates the subclass and super calls the parent constructor or method.

quiz.q: Which statement about JavaScript objects is NOT correct?
options: Private fields are written with a hash prefix
Every object has its own copy of every method
Objects inherit through a prototype chain
class syntax is sugar over prototypes
quiz.why: Methods live on the prototype and are shared, which is why they are defined there.

quiz.q: What is polymorphism in this context?
options: A subclass replacing a parent method with its own version
quiz.why: The same call reaches different code depending on the object it is made on.

quiz.q: What does a static member belong to?
options: The class itself rather than an instance
quiz.why: A static member is reached through the class name, not through an object made from it.

card.examTip: Explain prototypes, compare constructors and class syntax, and describe inheritance and overriding.

topics.title: JSON
topics.definition: JavaScript Object Notation is a text format for exchanging structured data between a browser and a server.

children.title: JSON syntax rules
children.definition: Objects with quoted keys, arrays, strings, numbers, true, false and null, with no functions or comments.

children.title: JSON.parse and JSON.stringify
children.definition: Converting between a JSON string and a JavaScript object in both directions.

children.title: JSON versus XML
children.definition: JSON is lighter, easier to parse and native to JavaScript, while XML supports schemas, attributes and namespaces.

children.title: JSON in web APIs
children.definition: REST services send and receive JSON, which is the standard format of modern web APIs.

card.explanation: JSON is a text format for exchanging structured data between a browser and a server. Its syntax is deliberately small: objects with quoted keys, arrays, strings, numbers, and the literals true, false and null. Functions and comments are not allowed, and keys must be written in double quotes. Two methods do the conversion: JSON.parse turns a JSON string into a JavaScript object, and JSON.stringify does the reverse. Compared with XML it is lighter, easier to read and native to JavaScript, while XML still offers schemas, attributes and namespaces. Nearly every modern web API sends and receives JSON.
card.example: A weather API returns a JSON object with a temperature field. One parse call turns it into something a script can read.

quiz.q: Which method turns a JSON string into an object?
quiz.why: parse reads the text and builds the matching JavaScript value.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT valid in JSON?
quiz.why: JSON carries data only, so functions and comments cannot appear in it.

quiz.q: Which statement about JSON is NOT correct?
options: It supports true, false and null
quiz.why: Comments were removed from the format deliberately, to keep it simple.

quiz.q: Compared with XML, JSON is:
options: Able to use attributes and namespaces
Lighter and easier to parse in JavaScript
quiz.why: Its size and direct mapping to JavaScript objects are why APIs prefer it.

quiz.q: What does JSON.stringify produce?
quiz.why: It serialises a value into the text form that can be sent over the network.

card.examTip: State the JSON syntax rules, give both conversion methods, and compare JSON with XML.

topics.title: jQuery
topics.definition: jQuery is a small JavaScript library that simplifies DOM traversal, events, animation and AJAX.

children.title: Selectors and chaining
children.definition: The jQuery function selects elements with CSS style selectors and methods can be chained.

children.title: DOM manipulation and effects
children.definition: text, html, attr, addClass, append, remove, show, hide, fadeIn and slideToggle.

children.title: Events in jQuery
children.definition: on, click, hover and ready centralise event handling with the shorthand dollar ready function.

children.title: AJAX helpers
children.definition: get, post and ajax methods wrap XMLHttpRequest for short code.

children.title: Advantages and disadvantages
children.definition: Cross browser convenience and a large plugin base versus extra download size and reduced need today.

card.explanation: jQuery is a small library that simplifies DOM traversal, events, animation and AJAX. Its central idea is the jQuery function, usually written with a dollar sign, which selects elements with CSS style selectors. Methods can then be chained, so several operations read as one line. Manipulation covers text, html, attr, addClass, append and remove, and effects include show, hide, fadeIn and slideToggle. Events are handled with on, click, hover and ready, the last of which waits for the document. AJAX helpers wrap XMLHttpRequest in short calls: get, post and ajax. The trade off is an extra download, and much of what it offered is now built into the browser.
card.example: Hiding all error messages takes one line in jQuery. The same work in plain DOM code needs a loop.

quiz.q: What does the dollar sign function do in jQuery?
options: Selects elements with CSS style selectors
quiz.why: Selection is the entry point to everything else, and the result can be chained.

quiz.q: Which jQuery method waits until the document is ready?
quiz.why: Running code only after the document is parsed avoids null element errors.

quiz.q: Which statement about jQuery is NOT correct?
options: It adds an extra file to download
It is required for modern JavaScript to run
quiz.why: Browsers now provide querySelector, fetch and classList, so the library is often unnecessary.

quiz.q: Which is a jQuery effect method?
quiz.why: fadeIn animates visibility, while the others change content or attributes.

quiz.q: What does the jQuery ajax method wrap?
quiz.why: It hides the details of creating a request object and reading its state.

card.examTip: Describe selection and chaining, name four effect methods, and give one advantage and one drawback.

topics.title: AJAX
topics.definition: AJAX updates part of a page by exchanging data with the server in the background without reloading the page.

children.title: How AJAX works
children.definition: JavaScript sends an asynchronous request, the server replies with data, and the DOM is updated from the response.

children.title: XMLHttpRequest steps
children.definition: Create the object, open the request, set the callback, send it, then read readyState and status in the handler.

children.title: The fetch API and promises
children.definition: fetch returns a promise with json and text methods, used with async and await for cleaner code.

children.title: Same origin policy and CORS
children.definition: Cross origin requests are blocked unless the server allows them with CORS headers.

children.title: Advantages and issues
children.definition: Smoother interfaces and less data transfer, but bookmarking, history and search engine indexing become harder.

card.explanation: AJAX updates part of a page by exchanging data with the server in the background, without reloading the page. The sequence is always the same. Script sends an asynchronous request, the server replies with data, and the page updates from it. With XMLHttpRequest the steps are to create the object, open the request and set a callback. The handler then checks readyState and status before reading the response. The fetch API is the modern alternative: it returns a promise and is usually written with async and await. One rule governs cross site requests: the same origin policy blocks them unless the server allows them with CORS headers.
card.example: Typing in a search box and seeing suggestions appear, with the page never reloading, is AJAX at work.

quiz.q: What does AJAX allow a page to do?
options: Update part of the page using server data without a reload
quiz.why: The request happens in the background and only the changed part is redrawn.

quiz.q: What does the fetch API return?
quiz.why: The promise resolves to a response, whose json method gives the parsed data.

quiz.q: Which statement about AJAX is NOT correct?
options: AJAX requires the page to reload to show new data
readyState and status are checked in the handler
CORS headers let a server permit cross origin requests
quiz.why: Avoiding that reload is the entire purpose of the technique.

quiz.q: What does the same origin policy restrict?
options: Requests to a different origin unless CORS allows them
quiz.why: It is a browser security rule, and the server relaxes it by sending CORS headers.

quiz.q: Which method actually sends an XMLHttpRequest?
quiz.why: open configures the request and send transmits it.

card.examTip: Describe the AJAX cycle, the XMLHttpRequest steps, fetch with promises, and same origin with CORS.

topics.title: How the Web Works with PHP and the LAMP Stack
topics.definition: PHP is a server side scripting language that runs on the web server and outputs HTML.

children.title: Request response with PHP
children.definition: The browser requests a .php page, the server executes the script and returns the generated HTML.

children.title: Setting up the environment with LAMP
children.definition: Linux, Apache, MySQL and PHP form the classic free hosting stack, with XAMPP or WAMP for local practice.

children.title: PHP versus client side scripting
children.definition: PHP code runs on the server and the user never sees it, while JavaScript runs in the browser and is visible.

children.title: PHP file structure
children.definition: PHP code is written inside the opening and closing PHP tags and can be mixed with HTML.

card.explanation: PHP is a server side scripting language that runs on the web server and outputs HTML. The browser requests a page ending in php. The server executes the script and sends back only the generated HTML. The classic stack for this is LAMP: Linux, Apache, MySQL and PHP. XAMPP or WAMP gives the same combination on a local machine. The key contrast is with client side script. PHP runs on the server and the user never sees it, while JavaScript runs in the browser and is visible. PHP code sits inside its own opening and closing tags and can be mixed freely with markup.
card.example: Viewing the source of a PHP page in a browser shows HTML, never the PHP. That is the clearest proof of where it runs.

quiz.q: What does LAMP stand for?
quiz.why: The four components are the operating system, the server, the database and the language.

quiz.q: Where does PHP code run?
quiz.why: The server executes the script and sends only the result to the browser.

quiz.q: Which statement about PHP is NOT correct?
options: It can be mixed with markup
The user can read the PHP source in the browser
XAMPP provides a local development stack
quiz.why: Only the generated HTML is sent, so the source stays on the server.

quiz.q: Which tags surround PHP code?
options: Angle brackets with a question mark and php
quiz.why: The opening tag is the php marker and the closing tag ends the block.

quiz.q: Why can PHP keep a database password secret?
options: Because the code runs on the server and is never sent
quiz.why: Anything in the browser is visible, but server side code never reaches the client.

card.examTip: Describe the request cycle with PHP, expand LAMP, and contrast PHP with client side JavaScript.

topics.title: PHP Basics: Syntax, Variables and Constants
topics.definition: PHP scripts use loosely typed variables with a dollar sign and constants defined once.

children.title: Basic syntax and statements
children.definition: Statements end with a semicolon, comments use double slash, hash or block syntax, and case matters for variables.

children.title: Variables and scope
children.definition: Variables start with $, are dynamically typed, and have local, global and static scope with superglobals such as GET and POST.

children.title: Constants
children.definition: define and const create values that cannot change, and predefined constants include PHP_VERSION and __FILE__.

children.title: Data types and type juggling
children.definition: String, integer, float, boolean, array, object, null and resource, with automatic conversion in expressions.

card.explanation: PHP scripts use loosely typed variables, each written with a dollar sign in front of the name. Statements end with a semicolon, and comments use double slashes, a hash or block syntax. Variable names are case sensitive, which catches beginners out. Scope has three levels: local inside a function, global outside it, and static, which keeps a value between calls. Constants are created with define or const and cannot change. PHP supplies predefined constants such as the version and the current file. Values have types such as string, integer, float, boolean, array, object, null and resource, and PHP converts between them automatically in expressions.
card.example: A variable named count and one named Count are different things in PHP, which is not true of keywords.

quiz.q: How is a PHP variable written?
options: With a dollar sign before the name
With a hash before the name
quiz.why: The dollar sign is required on every variable, including when it is declared.

quiz.q: Which keyword keeps a local variable's value between function calls?
quiz.why: A static variable is initialised once and then remembers its value.

quiz.q: Which statement about PHP is NOT correct?
options: Constants can be redefined at any time
PHP converts types automatically in expressions
quiz.why: A constant is fixed once it is defined, which is the point of using one.

quiz.q: Which function creates a constant?
quiz.why: define creates a constant at run time, while const is used at compile time.

quiz.q: Which of these is a PHP data type?
quiz.why: A resource holds a handle to something external, such as an open database connection.

card.examTip: Show a variable declaration, list the variable scopes, and explain constants and type conversion.

topics.title: Print and Echo
topics.definition: PHP outputs content to the browser with echo, print, print_r and var_dump.

children.title: echo and print
children.definition: echo can take several arguments and is slightly faster, while print returns a value and takes one argument.

children.title: print_r and var_dump
children.definition: Debugging helpers that display arrays and objects in readable form.

children.title: printf and number formatting
children.definition: Formatted output with placeholders such as percent s, percent d and percent f.

children.title: Embedding output in HTML
children.definition: Short echo tags and heredoc syntax mix dynamic values into markup.

card.explanation: PHP sends content to the browser with several statements. echo can take several arguments and is marginally faster. print takes one argument and returns a value, so it can appear in an expression. For debugging, print_r shows an array or object in readable form, and var_dump goes further by adding types and lengths.
