Formatted output uses printf with placeholders for strings, integers and floating point numbers. Output is usually mixed into the page. Short echo tags and heredoc syntax let dynamic values sit inside markup without constant opening and closing of tags.
card.example: Printing a price to two decimal places is one printf call with a float placeholder, rather than manual rounding.

quiz.q: What is the difference between echo and print?
options: echo takes several arguments and returns nothing, print returns a value
quiz.why: Because print returns a value it can be used in an expression, while echo cannot.

quiz.q: Which function is best for debugging an array?
quiz.why: print_r shows the structure, while var_dump adds the type and length of each value.

quiz.q: Which statement about output is NOT correct?
options: Heredoc helps mix values into markup
echo can print only one value at a time
quiz.why: echo accepts several comma separated arguments, which is one of its small advantages.

quiz.q: Which placeholder would printf use for a whole number?
quiz.why: The integer placeholder prints a rounded whole number from the value given.

quiz.q: What does var_dump add beyond print_r?
options: The type and length of each value
quiz.why: Seeing the type is often what reveals why a comparison did not behave as expected.

card.examTip: Compare echo, print, print_r and var_dump, and give one use of printf and heredoc.

topics.title: Strings and Arrays in PHP
topics.definition: PHP offers many string functions and three kinds of arrays.

children.title: String functions
children.definition: strlen, strpos, substr, str_replace, strtoupper, trim, explode, implode and nl2br.

children.title: String interpolation
children.definition: Double quoted strings expand variables while single quoted strings do not.

children.title: Indexed arrays
children.definition: Arrays with numeric keys accessed by position, created with array or square brackets.

children.title: Associative arrays
children.definition: Arrays with named keys, used like records with field names.

children.title: Multidimensional arrays
children.definition: Arrays of arrays used for tables and grouped data.

children.title: Array functions
children.definition: count, sort, ksort, array_push, array_pop, array_merge, array_keys, array_values and foreach traversal.

card.explanation: PHP gives a large set of string functions: strlen, strpos, substr, str_replace, strtoupper, trim, explode, implode and nl2br. Interpolation is a useful detail. Double quoted strings expand variables in place, while single quoted strings do not. Arrays come in three kinds. An indexed array uses numeric keys. An associative array uses named keys, like a record. A multidimensional array holds arrays inside arrays, for tables of data. Traversal is usually done with foreach, and the common functions are count, sort, ksort, array_push, array_pop, array_merge, array_keys and array_values.
card.example: A row from a database arrives as an associative array, so a value is read by column name rather than position.

quiz.q: Which function splits a string into an array?
quiz.why: explode breaks a string at a separator, and implode joins the pieces back together.

quiz.q: Which array uses named keys?
quiz.why: Named keys let a value be read by field name, which suits a database row.

quiz.q: Which statement about PHP strings is NOT correct?
options: strlen changes the case of a string
Single quoted strings do not expand variables
quiz.why: strlen returns the length, while strtoupper is the function that changes case.

quiz.q: Which function counts the elements of an array?
quiz.why: count returns the number of elements and is the usual guard before a loop.

quiz.q: How does ksort differ from sort?
options: sort orders by key, ksort by value
ksort orders by key and keeps it, sort reindexes by value
quiz.why: ksort is what you want for an associative array, because sort would discard the keys.

card.examTip: Name five string functions, explain single and double quotes, and describe the three array kinds.

topics.title: Operators, Control Structures and Functions in PHP
topics.definition: PHP supports the usual operators, branches, loops and user defined functions.

children.title: Operators
children.definition: Arithmetic, assignment, comparison with == and ===, logical, increment, string concatenation with a dot and the null coalescing operator.

children.title: Conditional statements
children.definition: if, else, elseif, switch and the match expression.

children.title: Loops
children.definition: for, while, do while and foreach, with break and continue.

children.title: User defined functions
children.definition: Declared with the function keyword, with parameters, default values, variadic arguments, type hints and return values.

children.title: Include and require
children.definition: include and require reuse code from other files, with require stopping the script on failure.

children.title: Superglobals and sessions
children.definition: GET, POST, REQUEST, SERVER, COOKIE and SESSION carry data between requests.

card.explanation: PHP supports the usual operators, with two worth remembering. The dot joins strings, and the null coalescing operator gives a default when a value is missing. Comparison has loose and strict forms: double equals converts types, triple equals does not. Branching uses if, else, elseif and switch, and modern PHP also has the match expression. Loops include for, while, do while and foreach, with break and continue. Functions are declared with the function keyword. They may take defaults, variadic arguments, type hints and a declared return type. Other files are pulled in with include or require. require stops the script when the file is missing, while include only warns.
card.example: Requiring a database configuration file at the top of every page is standard, because a missing config should stop everything.

quiz.q: Which operator joins two strings in PHP?
quiz.why: The dot is concatenation, since plus is reserved for arithmetic.

quiz.q: What does the null coalescing operator do?
options: Provides a default when a value is missing or null
quiz.why: It shortens the common pattern of testing whether a key exists before using it.

quiz.q: Which statement about PHP is NOT correct?
options: include and require both insert another file
switch and match behave identically in every way
Triple equals compares without converting types
quiz.why: match returns a value and uses strict comparison, while switch uses loose comparison.

quiz.q: What is the difference between include and require?
options: include warns and continues, require stops the script on failure
quiz.why: A missing required file is a fatal error, which is what you want for configuration.

quiz.q: Which loop is used to walk through an array?
quiz.why: foreach gives each key and value without the bookkeeping of an index counter.

card.examTip: Name the string and null coalescing operators, compare == and ===, and explain include versus require.

topics.title: Reading Data in Web Pages
topics.definition: PHP reads user input from forms, URLs and cookies to build dynamic responses.

children.title: GET versus POST
children.definition: GET places data in the URL, is visible and limited in size; POST sends it in the request body and is safer for sensitive data.

children.title: Handling form input
children.definition: Reading the name attributes through the POST superglobal and validating each field on the server.

children.title: Validation and sanitisation
children.definition: filter_var, htmlspecialchars and trim defend against bad input, SQL injection and cross site scripting.

children.title: Uploading files
children.definition: The FILES superglobal with move_uploaded_file stores uploaded files after checking type and size.

children.title: Cookies and sessions
children.definition: setcookie stores small data on the client while session_start keeps server side state with a session id.

card.explanation: PHP reads user input from forms, URLs and cookies to build its response. The two methods differ sharply. GET places data in the URL, where it is visible and limited in size. POST sends it in the request body and suits sensitive or large data. A script reads each field through the POST or GET superglobal, using the control's name. Every value must then be validated and sanitised. trim, htmlspecialchars and filter_var defend against bad input, cross site scripting and SQL injection. Uploads arrive in the FILES superglobal and are stored with move_uploaded_file after checking type and size. State across requests is kept with cookies or sessions.
card.example: A contact form that posts to itself shows errors above the fields on the first attempt, then thanks the user.

quiz.q: When should GET be used?
options: For harmless data that can live in the URL, such as a search term
quiz.why: GET data is visible and has a length limit, so it suits searches and links.

quiz.q: Which function helps prevent cross site scripting when printing user input?
quiz.why: It escapes the characters that would otherwise become markup in the page.

quiz.q: Which statement about reading input is NOT correct?
options: Files arrive in the FILES superglobal
Sessions keep state on the server
GET is the safe way to send a password
POST data travels in the request body
quiz.why: A password in the URL is visible in the address bar, in logs and in browser history.

quiz.q: Which function stores an uploaded file?
quiz.why: It checks that the file really came from an upload before moving it into place.

quiz.q: What starts a session in PHP?
quiz.why: session_start must run before any output, because it sends a session cookie header.

card.examTip: Compare GET and POST, name three superglobals, and list three sanitising functions.

topics.title: Connecting PHP with MySQL
topics.definition: PHP connects to MySQL to store and retrieve application data with SQL statements.

children.title: Creating a connection
children.definition: mysqli_connect or new PDO with host, user, password and database name, plus error handling.

children.title: Executing queries
children.definition: mysqli_query or prepared statements run SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements.

children.title: Fetching results
children.definition: Associative and numeric fetch modes, mysqli_fetch_assoc, fetch_all and loops that print rows into a table.

children.title: Prepared statements
children.definition: Parameterised queries with bind_param or PDO bindValue prevent SQL injection.

children.title: Insert, update and delete with feedback
children.definition: Affected rows and insert id confirm the result of a data change.

children.title: Closing connections and error handling
children.definition: Frees results and closes the connection, with try catch or mysqli error checks for failures.

children.title: A small complete example
children.definition: A student form that inserts a record and lists all students joins HTML forms, PHP and MySQL end to end.

card.explanation: PHP connects to MySQL to store and retrieve data with SQL statements. A connection is made with mysqli_connect or by creating a PDO object. Both take the host, user, password and database name, and both can fail. Queries then run through mysqli_query or a prepared statement, whether they are SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE. Results come back as rows fetched with mysqli_fetch_assoc or fetch_all. They are usually printed into a table inside a loop. Prepared statements matter most. Binding parameters keeps user input out of the SQL and prevents injection. After a change, affected rows and the insert id confirm what happened. The connection is then closed.
card.example: A student form inserts a record, reads back the new id and then lists every student in a table.

quiz.q: Which practice prevents SQL injection?
quiz.why: The statement is sent first and the values separately, so input cannot change the SQL.

quiz.q: Which function fetches a result row as an associative array?
quiz.why: It returns one row at a time with column names as keys, which suits a loop.

quiz.q: Which statement about PHP and MySQL is NOT correct?
options: The insert id reports the key of a new row
Affected rows counts the rows a change touched
A connection never needs to be checked for failure
quiz.why: Connection failures are common, and an unchecked one produces confusing errors later.

quiz.q: Which value tells you how many rows an UPDATE changed?
options: The row count of the table
quiz.why: It is the standard way to report success back to the user after an edit.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of PDO over mysqli?
options: It works with several database systems through one interface
It writes the SQL for you
quiz.why: Switching database becomes a change of connection string rather than a rewrite.

card.examTip: Describe connecting, running a query, fetching rows, prepared statements and closing the connection.
